rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh raises the verb after حتى when it is detached from an asserted first action already completed; he uses the subjunctive when entry is intended as the endpoint.
rows.anchor: فإن جعلت الدخول في كل ذا غاية نصبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the claim that the subjunctive follows merely because the speaker is uncertain; even an explicit uncertainty adjunct does not require it.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أن النصب يكون في ذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He criticizes grammarians who force the subjunctive to avoid a perceived inversion: Arabs still raise after قد سرت.
rows.anchor: ليس في الدنيا عربي يرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With negated or rare little travel, raising presents entry as separate, while the subjunctive makes it the endpoint; قلما can negate many trips or much travel in one trip.
rows.anchor: ما سرت حتى أدخلها وحتى أدخلها

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says إنما سرت حتى أدخلها is awkward unless the trip is belittled; the wording otherwise gives no sign that the travel ended before entry.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الخليل | وتقول كان سيرى أمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb after حتى does not share the syntactic slot of the first verb as a verb after فاء does; it is detached like a clause after إذا or an introductory particle.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن ما بعد حتى لا يشرك الفعل الذي قبل حتى في موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After a nonasserted clause, حتى takes only the subjunctive because it reverts to أن or كي instead of acting as a clause-initial connector.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الفعل إذا كان غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أيهم سار حتى يدخلها allows raising because travel and entry are already asserted and only the actor is queried; أسرت حتى تدخلها requires subjunctive because no trip was affirmed.
rows.anchor: تقول أيهم سار حتى يدخلها لأنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In some contexts the present نفعل can stand for past فعلنا; a Sululi poem illustrates this, and أسير likewise means سرت when intended as past.
rows.anchor: فعلنا في بعض المواضع ومثل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With كان, an adverb like أمس can complete the first clause and permit raising after حتى; without a predicate for كان, that analysis fails.
rows.anchor: وتقول كان سيرى أمس سيرا متعبا حتى أدخلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh prefers raising generic nouns after أما because ordinary nouns do not behave like verbal nouns; أما العبيد فذو عبيد means one has a share among the slaves.
rows.anchor: ما ذكرت فى هذا باب أسماء والأسماء لا تجرى مجرى المصادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raised construction can be understood with an omitted preposition and phrase: أما من العبيد or أما في العبيد فأنت ذو عبيد.
rows.anchor: أما العبيد فأنت فيهم أو أنت منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أما ابن مزنية فأنا ابن مزنية can identify the second expression with the first; when the noun is circumstantial, accusative is also possible, as in صديقا or صاحبا.
rows.anchor: أما ابن مزنية فأنا ابن مزنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh allows accusative after أما when it is a circumstantial, as in أما صديقا فأنت صديق and أما صاحبا فأنت صاحب.
rows.anchor: كما قلت أما صديقا فأنت صديق

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yunus reports that some Arabs treat العبيد and العبد after أما like verbal nouns, yielding an accusative construction.
rows.anchor: وزعم يونس أن قوما من العرب يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh calls that usage rare and bad; the proper construction is raised, as Arabs, Abu Amr, and Yunus say, and he knows of no disagreement from al-Khalil.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يتكلم به وإنما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Applying the accusative analysis to أما العلم والعبيد is also ugly: it treats ordinary nouns as verbal nouns even though each alone should be raised.
rows.anchor: وهذا قبيح لأنك لو أفردته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When أما introduces a known, definite referent such as al-Harith or specific slaves, only raising works; the expression means there is no one of that identity beyond or apart from the known referent.
rows.anchor: فهذا لا يكون فيه أبدا إلا الرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أما أبوك فلك أب is likewise raised, understood as having a father in relation to or in the person of your father; accusative is unavailable.
rows.anchor: فهذا لا يكون فيه أبدا إلا الرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أن plus its verb functions like a verbal noun in أما أن يكون عالما; the verse's أن أخالفكم is likewise an infinitival complement. Sibawayh cites لئلا يعلم أهل الكتاب as parallel evidence.
rows.anchor: أن مع الفعل الذى يكون صلة بمنزلة المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The أن clause is not circumstantial: it refers to what is to happen afterward, rather than describing the first event as it occurs.
rows.anchor: ولا تقع أن وصلتها حالا يكون الأول فى حال وقوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh distinguishes conditional nouns and adverbs such as من، ما، أي، متى، أين and أنى from the particles إن، إذما; elsewhere, adding ما turns certain temporal or spatial forms into conditionals.
rows.anchor: فما يجازى به من الأسماء غير الظروف من وما وأيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: حيث alone is not conditional because the following clause completes it as a relative place phrase; حيثما becomes conditional when ما changes its construction.
rows.anchor: حيث أن يجازى بها أنك تقول حيث تكون أكون فتكون وصل لها

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil analyzes مهما as ما joined to another redundant ما, by analogy with متى ما، إن ما، أينما and أيًّا ما; Quran 17:110 exemplifies the last pattern.
rows.anchor: وسألت الخليل عن مهما فقال هي ما

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says كيف تصنع أصنع is an awkward expression, not a conditional particle, though its meaning is conditional: however you act, I act.
rows.anchor: وسألت الخليل عن قوله كيف تصنع أصنع فقال هي مستكرهة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil distinguishes إذا from إن: إذا points to a known time, while إن is indefinite; poetic uses of إذا as a conditional particle are forced, and ordinary إذا ما is sound.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن إذا ما منعهم أن يجازوا بها فقال الفعل في إذا بمنزلته في إذ

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil calls إن the mother of conditional particles because it always remains conditional, while other particles can become interrogative or lose conditional force.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أن إن هي أم حروف الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional answer must be a verb or a clause introduced by فاء; و and ثم cannot introduce it.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه لا يكون جواب الجزاء إلا بفعل أو بالفاء

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil treats إذا هم يقنطون as linked to the preceding conditional and occupying the answer's place, like a verbal answer or one introduced by فاء; he compares أم أنتم صامتون with أم صمتم.
rows.anchor: فقال هذا كلام معلق بالكلام الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nominal answer such as إن تأتني أنا كريم is not acceptable in ordinary speech because it begins a new sentence without فاء or إذا; poets Hassan ibn Thabit and an al-Asadi poet use it by compulsion.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن قوله إن تأتني أنا كريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional followed by لأفعلن is normally bad because the oath answer starts independently; the Quranic examples work because the oath's lām is explicit or understood in لئن.
rows.anchor: من قبل أن لأفعلن تجيء مبتدأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry permits placing the conditional answer before its condition when the answer's position remains understood; Sibawayh cites Quran 11:15 as an answer that occupies the expected jussive slot without overt jussive marking.
rows.anchor: وقد تقول إن أتيتني آتيك أي آتيك إن أتيتني قال زهير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fa-introduced answer may be raised when it rests on an implied nominal clause, as in إن تأتني فأكرمك meaning فأنا أكرمك; Quranic examples use the same construction.
rows.anchor: فلا بد من رفع فأكرمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expressions such as حمدا، شكرا، عجبا and كرامة are accusatives governed by an omitted verb; they replace explicit forms such as أحمد الله or أشكر الله.
rows.anchor: فإنما ينتصب هذا على إضمار الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yunus reports that Ru'bah recited a line with عجب raised; Sibawayh uses it to show that such expressions can instead form a nominal clause.
rows.anchor: كان ينشد هذا البيت رفعا وهو لبعض مذحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A trusted Arab's reply حمد الله وثناء عليه is raised as a nominal statement, with an implied topic such as أمري or شأني, rather than an omitted verb.
rows.anchor: فيقول حمد الله وثناء عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh reads معذرة in قالوا معذرة إلى ربكم as a raised predicate: their admonition is an excuse to their Lord; if it meant a fresh apology, it would be accusative.
rows.anchor: ومثله فى أنه على الابتداء وليس على فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh parses فصبر جميل as a raised nominal clause meaning الأمر صبر جميل; the accusative version is more common and apt when directly exhorting someone.
rows.anchor: كأنه ~~يقول الأمر صبر جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In examples such as من أنت زيد, Arabic can omit the raising topic just as it omits the verb in accusative expressions, preserving the intended nominal sense.
rows.anchor: فتركوا إظهار الرافع كترك إظهار الناصب
